Figures follow the dashboard's own count, in which the two officer-training rows earn a single goal, as do the two administrative rows. Select any row for the club's full record.
Goals achieved so far this year, across all clubs. Five goals is Distinguished. Early in the year most clubs sit at zero, which is normal; read the ceiling rather than the count.
Share of clubs that have met each goal so far in {year}, as of {date}. Sorted worst first, so the top of this list is where district support buys the most goals before 30 June.
Climbed is a club that finished under five goals and then beat that score; slipped is a club that was above five and fell back. Five is the Distinguished threshold, which is why it is the pivot.

Most goals stay open until 30 June, but the officer-training and administrative windows close during the year. Each row is a window about to close, and the count is how many clubs have not met it yet.
This is the open program year as the dashboard reports it today, read across the whole district. For the clubs themselves, Every Area, Year by Year below carries this year beside the finished ones.

Everything below still stands: the real year-end results for the clubs this district held, kept because dissolving a district does not undo what its clubs did. Clubs carry on under whichever district took them.
This district was last listed by Toastmasters in its final year. It no longer exists, so the Year in Progress section is absent and there is no in-year workbook.
One row per club with the twelve goal counts, membership, ceiling and next deadline, filterable by division and area, built for an area director to open alongside a club officer.

No Success Plan narrows the table to clubs the dashboard has not recorded a Club Success Plan for. It is a prerequisite for every recognition level, so a club without one cannot be Distinguished however many goals it meets.

Ten squares per club, one per DCP goal. On the year still running, filled means achieved, outlined means still reachable and flat means the window has closed for good. On a finished year nothing is reachable any more, so a square is filled or it is not.

A handful of archived years record fewer goal rows than the score the dashboard gave the club, almost always a blank Jun–Aug officer-training row. The score is the dashboard's own and stands, and those rows are marked because the squares cannot account for it.

One row per club with its score in every year including the one still running, its latest recognition and membership, and a second sheet carrying the twelve goal counts per club-year, each marked as closed or still open.

The trace shows the shape of each club's run — steady, spiking or sliding — against a dashed line at five goals. The last column is the year still running, so it is goals met so far rather than a year-end score, and it moves with each dashboard snapshot.

On the year still running, a share measures pace. A goal almost nobody has met by October is not a goal going missing, so the bars are unbanded and their order is what to read. The Five-Year Trajectory beside them always spans every finished year, whichever one is picked.
Built from dashboards.toastmasters.org, District 21 club performance exports. Figures are year-end (30 June), and a club is listed under the district that held it in that year.

A club number survives a realignment and a district does not, so a club that transferred in brings its record with it. Those years show in a lighter figure, underlined: the score is the club's, but it was earned under the district that held it then, which the cell names on hover. A dash means no district recorded a score for that club that year, usually one before it chartered.

The last pill is the year still running, so a division or area leader can read the same grid for where their clubs stand now. That score is partial, so it is not banded the way a finished year is. Colour marks only what the year has already settled: recognition banked, Distinguished put out of reach, or a deadline inside 30 days. Everything else is a rank, worst at the foot of each area, which is where to start.
